chunks: Gyroscope vs accelerometer, why pair them. The question: What is the difference between a gyroscope and accelerometer? Why are they often used together?
A gyroscope measures how fast something rotates. An accelerometer measures pushes, and gravity is one of them.
Each can be used to work out tilt, and each fails in an opposite way. The gyro is smooth but slowly drifts off.
The accelerometer is right on average but gets fooled whenever the device speeds up.
Imagine a watch that is smooth and precise but gains a little time every minute.
You also have a radio time signal that is correct on average but crackly, so any single reading is noisy.
You trust the watch from moment to moment, and nudge it slowly toward the radio, so the crackle never makes the hands jump.
The gyro is the watch and the accelerometer is the radio.
One catch the picture hides: for turning about the vertical, like shaking your head "no", the accelerometer gives no "radio" at all, because gravity looks the same whichever way you face.
Red: a 0. 5 °/s bias gives 30° of error after 60 seconds. Orange: gyro noise alone is negligible (0. 08° at 60 seconds), so bias, not noise, is the problem.
Blue: the accelerometer is wrong by 16. 7° only while a 0. 3 g acceleration lasts, then recovers. Green: the complementary filter caps the bias error at 0.
245° at the cost of temporary accelerometer influence.
Gyroscope and accelerometer: see "What is a gyroscope / accelerometer?" for how each works. Bias: a small constant error in a sensor's output, even when the true input is zero.
Integrate: add up readings over time. Adding up the gyro's rotation rate gives an angle. Linear acceleration: speeding up or slowing down in a straight line.
Complementary filter: the watch-and-radio blend: mostly gyro in the short term, accelerometer in the long term.
A device sits still, but its gyro has a bias of 0. 5 degrees per second. Adding that up gives 30 degrees of false tilt after 60 seconds.
Now put the same sensors in a car speeding up at 0. 3 g. An accelerometer alone would claim a tilt of about 17 degrees.
The blend keeps the gyro's smooth short-term motion and lets the accelerometer pull the angle back slowly. That is the whole idea.
"An accelerometer measures specific force, so at rest it gives an absolute gravity reference for tilt with no drift, but it is noisy and corrupted by real acceleration.
A gyroscope measures rotation rate, so integrating it gives a smooth, responsive angle, but bias integrates into unbounded drift.
Their errors are complementary, so a complementary or Kalman filter trusts the gyro at high frequency and the accelerometer at low frequency.
Neither can fix yaw when level, so a magnetometer is added."
